solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Excluding that French boat

blocks.note: bar as a preposition means except or excluding, as in 'bar none'
que is French for the conjunction 'that'

explanation.surface: Turning away a little craft from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excluding' reads as an instruction to remove something, but it simply supplies the preposition bar. 'That French' asks for the French word for that.
explanation.definitionFit: A barque is a sailing vessel with three or more masts, a particular kind of ship.

clue.text: Nervous harbour master rears out of Welsh resort

indicators.note: a nervous person is jittery and unsettled, so the letters are agitated into a new order
taking something out of a collection leaves the rest behind, so some letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A jittery port official keeps rising up and leaving a Welsh seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike R, E, A, R and S from HARBOURMASTER and the eight letters left rearrange to BARMOUTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmouth is a seaside holiday town on the coast of Gwynedd in north-west Wales.

clue.text: Artist and couturier accept French madman in channel

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist
Christian Dior, the French fashion designer
fou is French for mad or a madman

explanation.surface: A painter and a fashion designer let a French lunatic join them somewhere along a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' looks like a stretch of water in the surface but it is the broadcasting sense. Radio Four is the BBC's main speech radio station in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcasting channel is a station, and BBC Radio Four is one of the national radio services.

clue.text: Fleas heading off to gorse

indicators.note: with its head taken off, a word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: Pulex is the Latin genus name of the common flea

explanation.surface: Fleas leaving for a patch of prickly shrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver needs the scientific name: Pulex is the flea genus, and Ulex the gorse genus, so one botanical Latin name turns into another by dropping P.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulex is the botanical genus to which gorse, the spiny yellow-flowered shrub, belongs.

clue.text: Broad avenues to out-of-town stations

blocks.note: first meaning: wide landscaped roads
second meaning: British railway stations on the edge of a town with large car parks, such as Bristol Parkway

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, a Parkway station is a railway station built outside a town for drivers to park and ride, such as Bristol Parkway.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both wide tree-lined roads and the park-and-ride railway stations built on town outskirts.

clue.text: Better than expected, but not for Tiger, say

blocks.note: surface reading: an everyday phrase for a performance that beats the norm
setter's reading: in golf, Tiger Woods' sport, a score over the standard is bad, so the phrase is reversed

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means better than average, but a golfer such as Tiger Woods wants to score below the standard for a hole, so for him it is worse.
explanation.definitionFit: Par is the expected standard, so anything over it in ordinary use means superior to normal expectations.

clue.text: Fake quakes, awfully reminiscent of a Czech novelist

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Staged earthquakes feel nightmarishly like something out of a Prague writer's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of the first two words rearrange to the adjective; the surface itself is already rather nightmarish.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Kafka was a Prague-born writer, and the adjective describes surreal, oppressive situations like those in his books.

clue.text: One sailor and another with no joint is surprised, when taken

indicators.note: having none of something means it has been taken away

blocks.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman, a single sailor
a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor
J is slang for a cannabis joint

explanation.surface: One seaman is startled when a shipmate turns up without his cannabis cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole idiom: taken aback means surprised, so the word fills the gap in 'surprised, when taken ...'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'taken aback' means startled or disconcerted, so the word completes that fixed phrase.

clue.text: Inwardly composed, at ease, calm

indicators.note: inwardly points to what lies inside the following words rather than the words themselves

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A description of someone serene within: composed, relaxed and calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface seems to mean calm, which hides that 'composed' and 'at ease' are only the container of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate describes a person who is quiet, unhurried and dignified, which is a synonym of tranquil.

clue.text: Bone discovered in Roman villa

indicators.note: something discovered inside a place was lying within it, so the letters lie within the phrase

blocks.note: the letters span the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Archaeologists dig up a bone at the site of an ancient Roman house.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaeological picture makes you think of a skeleton; the bone is the tiny one in the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The anvil, or incus, is one of the three small ossicles of the middle ear, so it is a bone.

clue.text: Hewlett Johnson meandered around without me

indicators.note: turned around in every direction, the letters are rearranged
going without something means losing it, so letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A churchman wandered about somewhere, leaving the speaker behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meandered around' together suggests a wander, but 'around' is the anagram signal and 'meandered' its fodder once ME goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewlett Johnson, Dean of Canterbury from 1931 to 1963, was nicknamed for his open support of Soviet communism.

clue.text: Cavalier has gone to help

blocks.note: someone who has gone off has left
to lend a hand is to help

explanation.surface: A Royalist soldier from the Civil War has left to lend assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital makes 'Cavalier' look like a Royalist of the English Civil War; here it is the adjective meaning dismissive.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a casual, brusque manner that shows little care or courtesy towards others.

clue.text: Small shire and bullock working

blocks.note: a bullock is a castrated bull, an ox
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A little rural county with a hard-working bullock in the fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' signals an abbreviation: Oxon is the short form of Oxfordshire, an English county west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxon is the standard shortened name for Oxfordshire, and shire is another word for county.

clue.text: Cover for Mae West’s biography?

blocks.note: surface reading: the dust wrapper on a book about the film star
setter's reading: Mae West was wartime slang for an inflatable buoyancy vest, and a biography is a story of someone's years

explanation.walkthrough: RAF airmen nicknamed their inflatable vests Mae Wests after the buxom actress, so the flotation garment and a biography's dust wrapper share one name.
explanation.definitionFit: The flotation vest nicknamed a Mae West is this item, and a biography's book cover is literally its name too.

clue.text: Two happy dogs heard in city on the Murrumbidgee

indicators.note: what is heard is what is spoken, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: a happy dog wags its tail, so each is a wagger

explanation.surface: A pair of contented dogs can be heard barking in an Australian river town.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic accent, wagger and wagga sound the same, so two waggers give the doubled place name.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagga Wagga is the largest inland city of New South Wales, Australia, standing on the Murrumbidgee River.

clue.text: It corrupts data of half the company at start of the year

indicators.note: taking only half of something means discarding the remainder

blocks.note: a troupe is a company of performers
JAN, short for January, is the opening month

explanation.surface: Some malware wrecked records for half the firm's staff in early January.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the front half of TROUPE is kept. A Trojan horse in computing is malicious software disguised as something harmless.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trojan is malicious software that poses as a legitimate program and then damages or steals files on a computer.

clue.text: Employee’s docket settles insolence

blocks.note: to settle a bill is to pay it
lip is cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: A worker's paperwork deals with some cheeky behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settles' looks like the verb of the surface sentence, but it is merely a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A payslip is the note an employer gives each worker showing wages and deductions, a kind of docket.

clue.text: Airline troubled by travelling youths, at first, undoubtedly

indicators.note: something troubled is disturbed, so the letters are thrown into disorder
at first points to the opening letter of each word

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A carrier is plagued by young backpackers, without any doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travelling' seems to describe the youths but only gives its own first letter. The definition sits at the end after a comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions affirm that something is actually true, as opposed to how it might appear.

clue.text: Ship holding right pennant

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a steamer is a steamship
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A vessel flying the correct flag.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of a ship and a flag fits so well that 'Ship' reads as part of the definition, but it supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennant is a long narrow flag, and a streamer is a long ribbon-like flag flown from a mast.

clue.text: From outskirts of Suez to Czechoslovakia, round Nice to Polish city

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so only the outermost letters are kept
to turn round is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the first and last letters
CZ was the international vehicle code for Czechoslovakia
taken as written

explanation.surface: A European itinerary: from Egypt to central Europe, via the Riviera, ending in Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: The travel picture makes 'to' look like part of the route, but the second one introduces the definition. Szczecin is the Baltic port once called Stettin.
explanation.definitionFit: Szczecin is a major port in north-west Poland near the German border, formerly the German city of Stettin.

clue.text: Early aviators correct in two ways

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: W and S, west and south, are two compass directions
right means correct

explanation.surface: Pioneering fliers were proved right on two counts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct in two ways' reads as a single phrase meaning doubly right; here 'ways' means compass directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903, making them pioneers of flying.

clue.text: Common mineral measures we’re told

indicators.note: what we are told reaches us by ear, so the sound counts and not the spelling

blocks.note: quarts are measures of liquid, each two pints

explanation.surface: Someone is told how much of a widespread mineral there is.
explanation.walkthrough: Quarts, the liquid measures, are pronounced exactly like the mineral's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Quartz, crystalline silica, is one of the most abundant minerals in the Earth's crust.

clue.text: Musical seen in Texan ad, unusually

indicators.note: what is seen in something is visible within it, so the letters lie inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run from the third word's end through to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A stage show turns up in an advertisement from Texas, oddly enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the text containing the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Xanadu is a 1980 roller-disco film starring Olivia Newton-John, later adapted as a Broadway stage show.

clue.text: Coopers’ tools regularly rejected in sleazy deal

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is taken
something rejected is sent back, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: Barrel-makers' equipment keeps being turned down in a shady transaction.
explanation.walkthrough: A cooper makes wooden barrels and shapes the staves with these arched cutting tools.
explanation.definitionFit: An adze is an axe-like tool with a blade set at right angles to its handle, used by coopers for shaping wood.

clue.text: Battle relics or hardware. So unusual

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters are out of their normal order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Leftovers from a battlefield, or metal gear: that's rare.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stop splits the fodder across two sentences; 'or' is the link between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrowheads are the stone or metal tips of arrows often recovered from ancient battlefields, so they are old remains of fighting.

clue.text: Spoke of island ways

indicators.note: something spoken is uttered out loud, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: Rhodes is a Greek island in the Aegean

explanation.surface: Someone talked about routes on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' could be the part of a wheel, but it is the past tense of speak, telling you to say the island's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A way is a route or track, and roads are routes along which people travel.

clue.text: Apple’s music

blocks.note: first meaning: a variety of eating apple sold under this brand name
second meaning: the improvised style that originated in New Orleans

explanation.walkthrough: The capital A and possessive suggest the technology company and its music service; the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jazz is both a crisp red apple cultivar from New Zealand and a style of syncopated, improvised popular music.

clue.text: Granular snow seen during interview, evenly – even upwards

indicators.note: taken evenly, only the letters in the second, fourth and later paired places are kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
a confirming aside rather than extra letters: in a down entry, this word read from the bottom spells the same four letters

explanation.surface: Someone mentions a kind of snow during an interview, then something about evenness and rising.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'even upwards' is a second, confirming wordplay: in a down entry the word EVEN read from the bottom gives the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Névé is the compacted granular snow found at the head of a glacier, also called firn.

clue.text: Filling the morning arranging gala on First of May

indicators.note: arranging things puts them into a fresh order
the first of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a.m. denotes the morning
taken as written
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Spending the morning organising a festival on May Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' looks like a verb about passing the time, but it is a noun: what a dentist puts in a tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Dental amalgam is the mercury alloy traditionally used by dentists to fill cavities in teeth.

clue.text: Mournful key member CIA outed

indicators.note: being outed is being exposed and thrown into disarray, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: E is a musical key
a limb is a member of the body
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sorrow at an important agent of the American spy agency being exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key member' reads as one phrase meaning an important person; split, the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a lament for the dead, so the adjective describes something sorrowful and plaintive.

clue.text: Worried parachutists chat away on the first floor

indicators.note: a worried mind is in turmoil, so the letters are churned up
something sent away is no longer present, so letters are dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Nervous skydivers talk at length while waiting on an upper storey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chat away' reads as talking freely, but 'away' removes the letters of 'chat'. In Britain the first floor is the one above the ground floor.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage the first floor is one level above ground, so being there means being up a flight of steps.

clue.text: African knowledge not returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: ken is one's range of knowledge, as in 'beyond my ken'
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Someone from Africa finds their learning was not given back.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken, a Scottish and archaic word for knowledge, survives in the phrase 'beyond my ken'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Kenyan is a person from Kenya, a country in East Africa, so the word names one kind of African.
